extraction_notes.note: All pseudocode sits in table floats (tabular with 'N: &' rows), not algorithm environments, so latex_facts reports no lines and pseudocode_steps could not be used. Each algorithm spans caption to \end{tabular}; steps were cut by hand, one per printed line, with END lines dropped and loop/branch steps spanning their bodies. The 7 'ends mid-sentence' warnings on these spans are false alarms.

The GoP-deadline assumption appears twice (Sec. 3.5 with $N_G$, Sec. 4.2.1 with $T_{GoP}$). Both copies are kept because each introduces a symbol that later nodes use. The Sec. 3.3 timescale assumption is restated more fully in Sec. 5.3.5, so only AssumP22 is kept.
A \newtheorem{fact} environment stating a result cited from Bertsekas; typed as an external theorem (Hard rule 4), not as a claim.
The linear rate-PSNR model cited from van der Schaar could be a definition of $Q_l$ or a modeling assumption. Typed as an external definition because it introduces $Q_l$, $Q_l^b$ and $\beta_l$.

Each optimization problem is written as a numbered display. The problem node is the lead-in sentence plus the display, and the display stays a nested equation node. ProbP1 extends one sentence past the display, so that it ends at a sentence boundary.
The proportional-fairness sentence citing Kelly has no final period in the source, and Sec. 5.2 restates it without citation. One node was kept, the cited copy.
Not extracted: the related-work survey (Sec. 2), the simulation parameter settings, and the figure-by-figure discussion. Only the headline simulation findings became numerical claims.

nodes.name: M orthogonal channels
nodes.statement: We consider a spectrum band consisting of $M$ orthogonal channels with identical bandwidth~\cite{Jia08,Hu11MC}.

nodes.name: Channels allocated to K primary networks
nodes.statement: We assume that the $M$ channels are allocated to $K$ primary networks, which cover different service areas.

nodes.name: Synchronous primary slot structure
nodes.statement: We further assume that the primary systems use a synchronous slot structure as in prior work~\cite{Zhao07a, Su08}.

nodes.name: Markov channel occupancy
nodes.statement: Due to primary user transmissions, the occupancy of each channel evolves following a discrete-time Markov process, as validated by recent measurement studies~\cite{Zhao07a, Su08, Motamedi07}.
nodes.statement_short: Each channel's occupancy evolves as a discrete-time two-state Markov process.

nodes.name: Channel status $S_m^k(t)$
nodes.statement: In primary network $k$, the status of channel $m$ in time slot $t$ is denoted by $S_m^k(t)$ with idle (i.e., $S_m^k(t)=0$) and busy (i.e., $S_m^k(t)=1$) states.

nodes.name: Channel transition probabilities
nodes.statement: Let $\lambda_m^k$ and $\mu_m^k$ be the transition probability of remaining in state $0$ and that from state $1$ to $0$, respectively, for channel $m$ in primary network $k$.

nodes.name: Channel utilization $\eta_m^k$
nodes.statement: The utilization of channel $m$ in primary network $k$, denoted by $\eta_m^k = \Pr(S_m^k=1)$, is \begin{eqnarray} \eta_m^k = \lim_{T \to \infty} \frac{1}{T} \mbox{$\sum_{t=1}^T$} S_m^k(t) = \frac{1-\lambda_m^k}{1-\lambda_m^k+\mu_m^k}. \end{eqnarray}
nodes.statement_short: Utilization of a channel is its long-run busy fraction, $(1-\lambda)/(1-\lambda+\mu)$.

nodes.name: Infrastructure-based CR multicast setting
nodes.statement: As shown in Fig.~\ref{fig:ntwarch}, we consider a CR base station multicasts $G$ real-time videos to $G$ multicast groups, each of which have $N_g$ users, $g=1, 2, \cdots, G$.

nodes.name: Tile
nodes.statement: Note that a time slot and channel combination, termed a {\em tile}, is the minimum unit for resource allocation.
differentia: the minimum unit for resource allocation

nodes.name: Channel bonding at CR users
nodes.statement: Without loss of generality, we assume that each CR network user can access all the available channels with the channel bonding/aggregation techniques~\cite{Corderio06, Mahmoud09}.

nodes.name: CR node set $\mathcal{U}^k$
nodes.statement: Let $\mathcal{U}^k$ denote the set of CR nodes that are located within the coverage of primary network $k$.

nodes.name: Video session source and destination
nodes.statement: A video session $l$ may be relayed by multiple CR nodes if source $z_l$ is not a one-hop neighbor of destination $d_l$.

nodes.name: Common control channel
nodes.statement: We assume a {\em common control channel} for the CR network~\cite{Su08}.

nodes.name: Virtual tunnel
nodes.statement: In the transmission phase, the channels assigned to a video session $l$ at each link along the path form a virtual ``tunnel'' connecting source $z_l$ and destination $d_l$.
nodes.genus: the channels assigned to a video session $l$ at each link along the path

nodes.name: Amplify-and-forward relaying
nodes.statement: We adopt amplify-and-forward for video transmission~\cite{Laneman04}.

nodes.name: False alarm and miss detection
nodes.statement: A {\em false alarm} may lead to waste a spectrum opportunity and a {\em miss detection} may causes collision with primary users.

nodes.name: Hypotheses $H_0$ and $H_1$
nodes.statement: Denote $H_0$ as the hypothesis that channel $m$ in primary network $k$ is idle, and $H_1$ the hypothesis that channel $m$ in primary network $k$ is busy in time slot $t$.

nodes.name: Conditional channel availability $a_m^k(t)$
nodes.statement: The conditional probability that channel $m$ is available in primary network $k$, denoted by $a_m^k(t)$, can be derived as, \begin{eqnarray} a_m^k(t) &=& \Pr(H_0|W_i^m=\theta_i^m, \; i \in \mathcal{U}_m^k, \pi_m^k) \nonumber \\ &=& \left[ 1 + \left( \varphi_m^k \right)^{u_m^k} \left( \phi_m^k \right)^{|\mathcal{U}_m^k|-u_m^k} \frac{\Pr(H_1|\pi_m^k)}{\Pr(H_0|\pi_m^k)} \right]^{-1}. \end{eqnarray} where $\theta_i^m$ represents a specific sensing result (0 or 1), $\mathcal{U}_m^k$ is the subset of users in $\mathcal{U}^k$ (i.e., the set of CR nodes that are located within the coverage of primary network $k$) that sense channel $m$, $u_m^k$ is the number of users in $\mathcal{U}_m^k$ observing channel $m$ is idle, $\pi_m^k$ represents the history of channel $m$ in primary network $k$, and $\varphi_m^k$ and $\phi_m^k$ are defined as: \begin{eqnarray} \left\{ \begin{array}{ll} \varphi_m^k=\frac{P(W_i^m=0|H_1)}{P(W_i^m=0|H_0)}=\frac{\delta_m}{1-\epsilon_m}, & \mbox{when } \theta_i^m=0 \\ \phi_m^k=\frac{P(W_i^m=1|H_1)}{P(W_i^m=1|H_0)}=\frac{1-\delta_m}{\epsilon_m}, & \mbox{when } \theta_i^m=1 . \end{array}\right. \end{eqnarray}
nodes.statement_short: Posterior probability that a channel is idle given all CR users' sensing results and the channel history, via likelihood ratios $\varphi,\phi$.

nodes.name: Base and enhancement layer rates
nodes.statement: With FGS or MGS coding, each video $l$ is encoded into one base layer with rate $R_l^b$ and one enhancement layer with rate $R_l^e$.

nodes.name: Total video bit rate $R_l$
nodes.statement: The total bit rate for video $l$ is $R_l=R_l^b+R_l^e$.

nodes.name: Rate-PSNR model of scalable video
nodes.statement: As in prior work~\cite{Schaar03}, the average PSNR of video $l$, denoted as $Q_l$, can be estimated as: \begin{equation} Q_l(R_l) = Q_l^b + \beta_l(R_l - R_l^b) = Q_l^0 + \beta_l R_l, \end{equation} where $Q_l^b$ is the resulting PSNR when the base layer is decoded alone, $\beta_l$ a constant depending on the video sequence and codec setting, and $Q_l^0 = Q_l^b - \beta_l R_l^b$.
nodes.statement_short: Average PSNR of a scalable video is affine in its received rate, $Q_l = Q_l^0 + \beta_l R_l$.

nodes.name: GOP delivery deadline ($N_G$ slots)
nodes.statement: Due to the real-time nature, we assume that each {\em group of pictures} (GOP) must be delivered during the next GOP window, which consists of $N_G$ time slots.

nodes.name: Maximum allowed collision probability and transmission probability
nodes.statement: Let $\gamma_n \in (0, 1)$ be the {\em maximum allowed collision probability} with primary users on channel $n$, and $p^{tr}_n(t)$ the {\em transmission probability} on channel $n$ for the base station in time slot $t$.

nodes.name: Collision probability bound (infrastructure)
nodes.statement: The probability of collision caused by the base station should be kept below $\gamma_n$, i.e., $p^{tr}_n(t) \left[ 1 - a_n(t) \right] \le \gamma_n$.

nodes.name: Modulation-Coding (MC) schemes
nodes.statement: We consider $M$ unique combinations of modulation and FEC schemes, termed {\em Modulation-Coding} (MC) schemes, in this paper.

nodes.name: Ordered MC scheme list
nodes.statement: Let $\{MC_m\}_{m=1,\cdots,M}$ be the list of available MC schemes indexed according to their data rates in the increasing order.

nodes.name: Slow fading channels
nodes.statement: We assume slow fading channels with coherence time larger than a time slot.

nodes.name: Users decoding each MC scheme $n_{g,m}$
nodes.statement: At the beginning of a time slot, the base station is able to collect the number $n_{g,m}$ of users in each multicast group $g$ who can successfully decode $MC_m$ signals for $m=1, 2, \cdots, M$.

nodes.name: Base layer uses $MC_1$
nodes.statement: Without loss of generality, we assume that the base layer is always transmitted using $MC_1$.

nodes.name: Enhancement sub-layers
nodes.statement: We further divide the enhancement layer into $M$ sub-layers, where sub-layer $m$ has rate $R_{g,m}^e$ and uses $MC_m$.

nodes.name: Tiles per sub-layer $l_{g,m}$
nodes.statement: Assuming that $MC_m$ can carry $b_{g,m}$ bits of video $g$ in one tile, we denote the number of tiles for sub-layer $m$ of video $g$ as $l_{g,m} \geq 0$.

nodes.name: User utility $U_{g,i}$
nodes.statement: Since we consider video quality in this paper, we define the utility for user $i$ in group $g$ as $U_{g,i} = \log Q_{g,i} = \log \left( Q^b_g+\beta_g R^e_g(i) \right)$, where $R^e_g(i)$ is the received enhancement layer rate of user $i$ in group $g$.

nodes.name: Group utility $U_g$
nodes.statement: The total utility for group $g$ is $U_g = \sum_{i=1}^{N_g} U_{g,i}$.

nodes.name: System utility $U$
nodes.statement: The utility function of the entire CR video multicast system is \begin{equation} U = \sum_{g=1}^G U_g. \end{equation}

nodes.name: Proportional fairness of log-utility maximization
nodes.statement: Maximizing $U$ will achieve {\em proportional fairness} among the video sessions~\cite{Kelly98}
conclusions: Maximizing $U$ will achieve {\em proportional fairness} among the video sessions

nodes.name: FGS base and enhancement layers
nodes.statement: To address heterogeneous user channels, we adopt FGS to produce a base layer with rate $R^b_g$ and an enhancement layer with rate $\bar{R}_g^e$.

nodes.name: Prescribed base layer rate
nodes.statement: Without loss of generality, we assume $R^b_g$ is prescribed for an acceptable video quality, while $\bar{R}^e_g$ is set to a large value that is allowed by the codec.

nodes.name: Effective enhancement layer rate
nodes.statement: During transmission, we determine the {\em effective rate} for each enhancement layer $R_g^e \leq \bar{R}^e_g$ depending on channel availability, sensing, and MC schemes.

nodes.name: GoP delivery deadline ($T_{GoP}$ slots)
nodes.statement: We assume that the data from a GoP should be be delivered in the next GoP window consisting of $T_{GoP}$ time slots.

nodes.name: Layered transmission order in a GoP window
nodes.statement: At the beginning of each GoP window, all the base layers are transmitted using the available tiles. {\em Retransmissions} will be scheduled if no ACK is received for a base layer packet. After the base layers are transmitted, we allocate the remaining available tiles in the GoP window for the enhancement layer. The same rule applies to the enhancement sub-layers, such that a higher sub-layer will be transmitted if and only if all the lower sub-layers are acknowledged.
nodes.statement_short: Send all base layers first with retransmissions, then fill remaining tiles with enhancement sub-layers in order of decoding dependency.

nodes.name: Opportunistic spectrum access scheme
nodes.statement: In each time slot $t$, the base station opportunistically access every channel $n$ with probability $p_n^{tr}(t)$ given in (\ref{eq:ptran}). Specifically, for each channel $n$, the base station generates a random number $x_n(t)$, which is independent of the channel history $\theta_n(t)$ and uniformly distributed in [0,1]. If $x_n(t) \leq p_n^{tr}(t)$, the most important packet among those not ACKed in the previous GoP will be transmitted on channel $n$. If an ACK is received for this packet at the end of time slot $t$, this packet is successfully received by at least one of the users and will be removed from the transmission buffer. Otherwise, there is a collision with primary user and this packet will remain in the transmission buffer and will be retransmitted.
nodes.statement_short: Per slot and channel, transmit the most important un-ACKed packet with probability $p_n^{tr}(t)$; drop it on ACK, keep it for retransmission otherwise.

nodes.name: Enhancement tile budget $T_e$ known
nodes.statement: We assume that the number of tiles used for the enhancement layers in a GoP window, $T_e$, is known at the beginning of the GoP window.
nodes.section: 4.2.2 Enhancement Layer Partitioning and Tile Allocation

nodes.name: OPT-Part
nodes.statement: Letting $\vec{l} = [l_{1,1}, l_{1,2}, \cdots, l_{1,M}, l_{2,1}, \cdots l_{G,M}]$ denote the {\em tile allocation vector}, we formulate an optimization problem OPT-Part as follows. \begin{eqnarray} \mbox{maximize:} && \hspace*{-0.2in} U(\vec{l}) = \sum_{g=1}^{G}\sum_{k=1}^M(n_{g,k}-n_{g,k+1}) \times \log \left[ Q^b_g+\beta_g \sum_{m=1}^k b_{g,m}l_{g,m} \right] \\ \mbox{subject to:} && \hspace*{-0.2in} \sum_{g=1}^G\sum_{m=1}^M l_{g,m}\le T_e \\ && \hspace*{-0.2in} \sum_{m=1}^M b_{g,m}l_{g,m} \le \bar{R}_g^e, \; g \in [1, \cdots, M] \\ && \hspace*{-0.2in} l_{g,m} \geq 0, \; m \in [1, \cdots, M], g \in [1, \cdots, G]. \end{eqnarray} OPT-Part is solved at the beginning of each GoP window to determine the optimal partition of the enhancement layer.
nodes.section: 4.2.2 Enhancement Layer Partitioning and Tile Allocation
nodes.statement_short: Choose tiles per sub-layer $l_{g,m}$ to maximize the proportional-fair log-PSNR utility under the tile budget $T_e$ and maximum rates.

nodes.name: NP-hardness of OPT-Part
nodes.statement: The formulated problem is a MINLP problem, which is NP-hard~\cite{Deb08}.
nodes.section: 4.2.2 Enhancement Layer Partitioning and Tile Allocation
assumptions: The formulated problem is a MINLP problem
conclusions: which is NP-hard

nodes.name: Reformulation-Linearization Technique (RLT)
nodes.statement: RLT is a technique that can be used to produce LP relaxations for a nonlinear, nonconvex polynomial programming problem.

nodes.name: Greedy algorithm GRD1
nodes.statement: \caption{The Greedy Algorithm (GRD1)} \begin{tabular}{ll} \hline 1: & Initialize $l_{g,m}=0$ for all $g$ and $m$ \\ 2: & Initialize $A=\{1,2,\cdots,G\}$\\ 3: & WHILE $\left( \sum_{g=1}^G\sum_{m=1}^Ml_{g,m} \le T_e \; \mbox{and } A \; \mbox{is not empty} \right)$ \\ 4: & $\;\;$ Find $l_{\hat{g},\hat{m}}$ that can be increased by one: \\ & $\;\;\;\;\;\;$ $\vec{e}_{\hat{g},\hat{m}}=\arg \max_{g \in A,m \in [1,\cdots,M]} \left\{ \frac{U(\vec{l}+\vec{e}_{g,m})-U(\vec{l})}{b_{g,m}+R/T_e} \right\}$ \\ 5: & $\;\;$ $\vec{l}=\vec{l}+\vec{e}_{\hat{g},\hat{m}}$ \\ 6: & $\;\;$ IF $\left( \sum_m b_{\hat{g},m}l_{\hat{g},m} > \bar{R}_g^e \right)$ \\ 7: & $\;\;\;\;\;\;$ $\vec{l}=\vec{l}-\vec{e}_{\hat{g},\hat{m}}$ \\ 8: & $\;\;\;\;\;\;$ Delete $\hat{g}$ from $A$ \\ 9: & $\;\;$ END IF \\ 10: & END WHILE \\ \hline \end{tabular}

nodes.statement_short: Greedily allocate tiles one at a time to the sub-layer with the largest normalized utility increase until tiles or video data run out.

nodes.name: Estimation horizon $T_{est}$
nodes.statement: It estimates the number of available tiles $T_e(t)$ in the next $T_{est}$ successive time slots, where $1 \le T_{est}\le T_{GoP}$ is a design parameter depending on the coherence time of the channels.

nodes.name: Estimated available tiles $T_e(t)$
nodes.statement: The number of available tiles in the following $T_{est}$ time slots can be estimated as $T_e(t) = \sum_{n=1}^N\sum_{\tau=0}^{t_{min}}\hat{a}_n(t+\tau)$, where $\hat{a}_n(t+0)=a_n(t)$ and $t_{min}=\min\{T_{est}-1,T_{GoP} - (t \; \mbox{mod} \; T_{GoP})\}$.

nodes.name: Complexity of GRD2
nodes.statement: For time slot $t$, the complexity of GRD2 is $O(MGK)$, where $K = | N_{ack}(t-1) - N_{ack}(t-2) + T_e(t)-T_e(t-1) |$.

conclusions: the complexity of GRD2 is $O(MGK)$, where $K = | N_{ack}(t-1) - N_{ack}(t-2) + T_e(t)-T_e(t-1) |$

A \mbox{ is not empty} \right]$ \\ 19: & \ \ \ \ \ \ Find $l_{\hat{g},\hat{m}}$ that can be increased by 1 \\ & \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ $\vec{e}_{\hat{g},\hat{m}}=\arg \max_{g \in A,m \in \{m',\cdots,M\}} \left\{\frac{U(\vec{l}+\vec{e}_{g,m})-U(\vec{l})}{b_{g,m}+R/T_e} \right\}$ \\ 20: & \ \ \ \ \ \ $\vec{l}=\vec{l}+\vec{e}_{\hat{g},\hat{m}}$ \\ 21: & \ \ \ \ \ \ IF $\left( \sum_m b_{\hat{g},m}l_{\hat{g},m} > \bar{R}^e_g \right)$ \\ 22: & \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ $\vec{l}=\vec{l}-\vec{e}_{\hat{g},\hat{m}}$ \\ 23: & \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ Delete $\hat{g}$ from $A$ \\ 24: & \ \ \ \ \ \ END IF \\ 25: & \ \ \ \ END WHILE \\ 26: & \ \ END IF \\ 27: & \ \ Update $N_{ack}(t-1)$ \\ 28: & END WHILE \\ \hline \end{tabular}

nodes.statement_short: Start from GRD1's allocation, then each slot re-estimate available tiles and greedily add or remove tiles of high sub-layers to track the estimate.

nodes.name: Utility increment $\mbox{Inc}(g,m,i)$
nodes.statement: We define $\mbox{Inc}(g,m,i)$ to be the increase in the group utility function $U(g)$ after the $i$-th tile in the sub-layer using $MC_m$ is successfully decoded.
nodes.section: 4.2.3 Tile Scheduling in a Time Slot

nodes.name: Closed form of $\mbox{Inc}(g,m,i)$
nodes.statement: It can be shown that $$ \mbox{Inc}(g,m,i) = \sum_{k=m}^M (n_{g,k}-n_{g,k+1}) \times \log \left[ 1+\frac{\beta_gb_{g,m}}{Q_g^b+\beta_g\sum_{u=1}^{m-1}b_{g,u}l_{g,u}+(i-1)\beta_gb_{g,m}} \right]. \nonumber $$
nodes.section: 4.2.3 Tile Scheduling in a Time Slot
nodes.statement_short: The increment from the $i$-th tile of sub-layer $m$ is a weighted sum of log ratios over user classes able to decode $MC_m$.

nodes.name: Tile success probability $c_n(t)$
nodes.statement: Letting $c_n(t)$ be the probability that the tile is successfully received, then we have $c_n(t) = p^{tr}_n(t) a_n(t)$.
nodes.section: 4.2.3 Tile Scheduling in a Time Slot

nodes.name: Tile scheduling problem
nodes.statement: Our objective of tile scheduling is to maximize the expected reward, i.e., \begin{eqnarray} \mbox{maximize:} \;\;\; \mbox{E} [\mbox{Reward}(\vec{\xi})] = \sum_{n=1}^N c_n(t) \cdot \mbox{Inc}(\xi_n), \end{eqnarray} where $\vec{\xi} = \{ \xi_n \}_{n=1,\cdots,N}$ and $\xi_n$ is the tile allocation for channel $n$, i.e., representing the three-tuple $\{g,m,i\}$.
nodes.section: 4.2.3 Tile Scheduling in a Time Slot
nodes.statement_short: Assign tiles to channels to maximize expected reward $\sum_n c_n(t)\,\mbox{Inc}(\xi_n)$.

nodes.name: Complexity of TSA
nodes.statement: The complexity of TSA is $O(N \log N)$.
nodes.section: 4.2.3 Tile Scheduling in a Time Slot
conclusions: The complexity of TSA is $O(N \log N)$.

nodes.name: Tile Scheduling Algorithm (TSA)
nodes.statement: \caption{Algorithm for Tile Scheduling in a Time Slot} \begin{tabular}{ll} \hline 1: & Initialize $m_g$ to the lowest MC that has not been ACKed for all $g$ \\ 2: & Initialize $i_g$ to the first packet that has not been ACKed for all $g$ \\ 3: & Sort $\{c_n(t)\}$ in decreasing order. Let the sorted channel list be \\ & \ \ indexed by $j$. \\ 4: & While ($j=1$ to $N$) \\ 5: & \ \ Find the group having the maximum increase in $U(g)$: \\ & \ \ \ \ \ $\hat{g}=\arg \max_{\forall g} \mbox{Inc}(g,m_g,i_g)$ \\ 6: & \ \ Allocate the tile on channel $j$ to group $\hat{g}$ \\ 7: & \ \ Update $m_{\hat{g}}$ and $i_{\hat{g}}$ \\ 8: & End while \\ \hline \end{tabular}
nodes.section: 4.2.3 Tile Scheduling in a Time Slot
nodes.statement_short: Sort channels by success probability and assign each, in order, to the group whose next tile has the largest utility increment.

nodes.name: Optimal ordering for tile scheduling
nodes.statement: E[Reward] is maximized if $\mbox{Inc}(\xi_i) > \mbox{Inc}(\xi_j)$ when $c_i(t) > c_j(t)$ for all $i$ and $j$.
nodes.section: 4.2.3 Tile Scheduling in a Time Slot
conclusions: E[Reward] is maximized
nodes.statement_short: Expected reward is maximized by pairing larger increments with more reliable channels.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 2 (tile scheduling order)
nodes.statement: Suppose there exists a pair of $i$ and $j$ where $\mbox{Inc}(\xi_i) > \mbox{Inc}(\xi_j)$ and $c_i(t) < c_j(t)$. We can further increase E[Reward] by switching the tile assignment, i.e., assign channel $i$ to $\xi_j$ and channel $j$ to $\xi_i$. With this new assignment, the net increase in E[Reward] is \begin{eqnarray} & & \hspace*{-0.3in} c_j(t)\mbox{Inc}(\xi_i) + c_i(t)\mbox{Inc}(\xi_j)-c_i(t)\mbox{Inc}(\xi_i)-c_j(t)\mbox{Inc}(\xi_j) \nonumber \\ & = & [c_j(t) - c_i(t)][\mbox{Inc}(\xi_i) - \mbox{Inc}(\xi_j)] > 0. \nonumber \end{eqnarray} Therefore E[Reward] is maximized when the $\{ \mbox{Inc}(\xi_i) \}$ and $\{c_i(t)\}$ are in the same order.
nodes.section: 4.2.3 Tile Scheduling in a Time Slot
nodes.statement_short: Exchange argument: swapping a mis-ordered pair strictly increases expected reward.

nodes.name: Greedy algorithm achieves best PSNR
nodes.statement: For all the groups, Greedy Algorithm achieves the best performance, with up to 4.2 dB improvements over Equal Allocation and up to 0.6 dB improvements over Sequential Fixing.
conclusions: Greedy Algorithm achieves the best performance, with up to 4.2 dB improvements over Equal Allocation and up to 0.6 dB improvements over Sequential Fixing

nodes.name: Video quality insensitive to sensing errors
nodes.statement: It is quite interesting to see that the video quality is not very sensitive to sensing errors. Even as $\epsilon_n$ is increased nine times from 10\% to 90\%, there is only 0.58 dB reduction (or a 1.5\% normalized reduction) in average PSNR when Greedy Algorithm is used.
conclusions: the video quality is not very sensitive to sensing errors

nodes.name: Spectrum access threshold $\kappa_m^k$
nodes.statement: Let $\kappa_m^k$ be a threshold for spectrum access: channel $m$ is considered idle if the estimate $a_m^k$ is greater than the threshold, and busy otherwise.

nodes.name: Channel availability $A_m^k$
nodes.statement: The availability of channel $m$ in primary network $k$, denoted as $A_m^k$, is \begin{eqnarray} A_m^k=\left\{ \begin{array}{ll} 0, & \mbox{$a_m^k \ge \kappa_m^k$}\\ 1, & \mbox{otherwise.}\\ \end{array}\right. \end{eqnarray}

nodes.name: Collision probability bound (multi-hop)
nodes.statement: For non-intrusive spectrum access, the collision probability should be bounded with a prescribed threshold $\gamma_m^k$.

nodes.name: Available channel set $\Omega_{i,j}$
nodes.statement: Let $\Omega_{i,j}$ be the set of available channels at link $\{i,j\}$. Assuming $i \in \mathcal{U}^k$ and $j \in \mathcal{U}^{k'}$, we have \begin{eqnarray} \Omega_{i,j} = \left\{ m \left| A_m^k=0 \mbox{ and } A_m^{k'}=0 \right. \right\}. \end{eqnarray}

nodes.name: Fixed link delay
nodes.statement: Assume each link has a fixed delay $\omega_{i,j}$ (i.e., processing and propagation delays).

nodes.name: All paths $\mathcal{P}_l^A$
nodes.statement: Let $\mathcal{P}_l^A$ be the set of all possible paths from $z_l$ to $d_l$.

nodes.name: Feasible path set $\mathcal{P}_l$
nodes.statement: For a given delay requirement $T_{th}$, the set of feasible paths $\mathcal{P}_l$ for video session $l$ can be determined as: \begin{eqnarray} \mathcal{P}_l = \left\{ \mathcal{P} \left| \sum_{\{i,j\} \in \mathcal{P}} \; \omega_{i,j} \le T_{th}, \; \mathcal{P} \in \mathcal{P}_l^A \right. \right\}. \end{eqnarray}

nodes.name: Channel packet loss rate $p_{i,j}^m$
nodes.statement: Let $p_{i,j}^m$ be the packet loss rate on channel $m$ at link $\{i,j\}$.

nodes.name: Link loss probability $p_{i,j}$
nodes.statement: The link loss probability $p_{i,j}$ can be derived as: \begin{eqnarray} p_{i,j} = 1 - \prod_{m \in \mathcal{M}} \; (1-p_{i,j}^m)^{I_m}, \end{eqnarray} where $\mathcal{M}$ is set of licensed channels and $I_m$ is an indicator: $I_m = 1$ if channel $m$ is used for the transmission, and $I_m = 0$ otherwise.

nodes.name: Path loss probability $p_l^h$
nodes.statement: Assuming independent link losses, the end-to-end loss probability for path $\mathcal{P}_l^h \in \mathcal{P}_l$ can be estimated as: \begin{eqnarray} p_l^h = 1 - \prod_{\{i,j\}\in \mathcal{P}_l^h} \; (1-p_{i,j}). \end{eqnarray}

nodes.name: Overall utility maximization
nodes.statement: Therefore, our objective is to maximize the overall system utility, i.e., \begin{equation} \mbox{maximize:} \;\; \sum_l U_l(R_l) = \sum_l \log (Q_l(R_l)). \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Maximize the sum of log-PSNRs of the video sessions (proportional fairness).

nodes.name: Channel scheduling indicator $x_{i,j,m}^{l,h,r}$
nodes.statement: We define two sets of index variables. For channel scheduling, we have \begin{eqnarray} x_{i,j,m}^{l,h,r}=\left\{ \begin{array}{ll} 1, & \mbox{at link $\{i,j\}$, if channel $m$ is} \\ & \mbox{assigned to tunnel $r$ in path $\mathcal{P}_l^h$} \\ 0, & \mbox{otherwise.} \end{array}\right. \end{eqnarray}
nodes.section: 5.2.1 Multi-hop CR Network Video Streaming Problem

nodes.name: Path selection indicator $y_l^h$
nodes.statement: For path selection, we have \begin{eqnarray} y_l^h=\left\{ \begin{array}{ll} 1, & \mbox{if video session $l$ selects path $\mathcal{P}_l^h \in \mathcal{P}_l$} \\ 0, & \mbox{otherwise}, \end{array}\right. \end{eqnarray}
nodes.section: 5.2.1 Multi-hop CR Network Video Streaming Problem

nodes.name: Dependence between indicators
nodes.statement: Note that the indicators, $x_{i,j,m}^{l,h,r}$ and $y_l^h$, are not independent. If $y_l^h=0$ for path $\mathcal{P}_l^h$, all the $x_{i,j,m}^{l,h,r}$'s on that path are $0$. If link $\{i,j\}$ is not on path $\mathcal{P}_l^h$, all its $x_{i,j,m}^{l,h,r}$'s are also $0$. For link $\{i,j\}$ on path $\mathcal{P}_l^h$, we can only choose those available channels in set $\Omega_{i,j}$ to schedule video transmission. That is, we have $x_{i,j,m}^{l,h,r} \in \{0, 1\}$ if $m \in \Omega_{i,j}$, and $x_{i,j,m}^{l,h,r} = 0$ otherwise.
nodes.section: 5.2.1 Multi-hop CR Network Video Streaming Problem
nodes.statement_short: Channel indicators vanish off the selected path and off available channels.

nodes.name: Vector forms $\mathbf{x}$, $\mathbf{y}$
nodes.statement: In the rest of the paper, we use $\mathbf{x}$ and $\mathbf{y}$ to represent the vector forms of $x_{i,j,m}^{l,h,r}$ and $y_l^h$, respectively.

nodes.name: Telescoping argument for per-slot maximization
nodes.statement: Since $\log(Q_l(\mbox{E}[R_l(0)]))$ is a constant, (\ref{eq:MaxQ}) is equivalent to the sum of utility increments of all the time slots, as \begin{eqnarray} && \hspace{-0.3in} \sum_l \log(Q_l(\mbox{E}[R_l(N_G)])) - \log(Q_l(\mbox{E}[R_l(0)])) \nonumber \\ && \hspace{-0.45in} = \sum_t \sum_l \left\{ \log(Q_l(\mbox{E}[R_l(t)])) - \log(Q_l(\mbox{E}[R_l(t-1)])) \right\}. \end{eqnarray}

nodes.statement_short: Telescope the utility over time slots: the end-of-window objective is the sum of per-slot increments.

nodes.name: Per-slot utility increment maximization
nodes.statement:
Therefore, (ef{eq:MaxQ}) will be maximized if we maximize the expected utility increment during each time slot, which can be written as:  egin{eqnarray} & & \hspace{-0.1in} \sum_l \log(Q_l(\mbox{E}[R_l(t)])) - \log(Q_l(\mbox{E}[R_l(t-1)])) 
onumber \ &=& \sum_l \log \left( 1 +  eta_l  rac{ \mbox{E}[R_l(t)] - \mbox{E}[R_l(t-1)] }{ Q_l(\mbox{E}[R_l(t-1)])} ight) 
onumber \ &=& \sum_l\sum_{h \in \mathcal{P}_l} y_l^h \log \hspace{-0.025in} \left( \hspace{-0.025in} 1 \hspace{-0.025in} + \hspace{-0.025in} \sum_r \sum_m  rac{ eta_l L_p x_{z_l, z'_l, m}^{l,h,r}}{N_G T_s Q_l^{t-1}} (1-p_{l,h}^r) \hspace{-0.025in} ight) 
onumber \ &=& \sum_l\sum_{h \in \mathcal{P}_l}y_l^h \log \hspace{-0.025in} \left( \hspace{-0.025in} 1 \hspace{-0.025in} + \hspace{-0.025in} ho_l^t \sum_r \sum_m x_{z_l,z'_l,m}^{l,h,r} (1-p_{l,h}^r) \hspace{-0.025in} ight), 
onumber \end{eqnarray} where $z'_l$ is the next hop from $z_l$ on path $\mathcal{P}_l^h$, $p_{l,h}^r$ is the packet loss rate on tunnel $r$ of path $\mathcal{P}_l^h$, $Q_l^{t-1} = Q_l(\mbox{E}[R_l(t-1)])$, and $ho_l^t =  eta_l L_p / (N_G T_s Q_l^{t-1})$.

conclusions: (\ref{eq:MaxQ}) will be maximized if we maximize the expected utility increment during each time slot

nodes.name: Disjointness weights $w_{l,h}^g$
nodes.statement: Such disjointedness constraint is also a special case of (\ref{eq:PathCon}) with the following definition for $w_{l,h}^g$ for each CR node $g$: \begin{equation} w_{l,h}^g = \left\{ \begin{array}{ll} 1, & \mbox{if node $g \in $ path $\mathcal{P}_l^h$} \\ 0, & \mbox{otherwise}, \end{array} \right. \end{equation}

nodes.name: OPT-CRV
nodes.statement: Finally we formulate the problem of multi-hop CR network video streaming (OPT-CRV) as: \begin{eqnarray} && \hspace{-0.4in} \mbox{max:} \;\; \sum_l \hspace{-0.03in} \sum_{h \in \mathcal{P}_l}y_l^h \log \hspace{-0.03in} \left( \hspace{-0.03in} 1 \hspace{-0.01in} + \hspace{-0.01in} \rho_l^t \sum_r \sum_m x_{z_l,z'_l,m}^{l,h,r} (1 \hspace{-0.01in} - \hspace{-0.01in} p_{l,h}^r) \hspace{-0.03in} \right) \\ && \hspace{-0.4in} \mbox{subject to:} \;\;\; (\ref{eq:DefX1}) \sim (\ref{eq:PathCon}). \nonumber \end{eqnarray}

assumptions: Problem OPT-CRV is in the form of MINLP (without continuous variables)
conclusions: which is NP-hard in general

nodes.name: Relaxed NLP of OPT-CRV
nodes.statement: We first obtain a relaxed {\em non-linear programming} (NLP) version of OPT-CRV. The binary variables $x_{i,j,m}^{l,h,r}$ and $y_l^h$ are relaxed to take values in [0,1]. The integer variables $n_l^h$ are treated as nonnegative real numbers.
nodes.statement_short: Relax binary variables to [0,1] and tunnel counts to nonnegative reals.

nodes.name: Relaxed OPT-CRV is convex
nodes.statement: It can be shown that the relaxed problem has a concave object function and the constraints are convex.
conclusions: the relaxed problem has a concave object function and the constraints are convex

nodes.name: Relaxation gives exact solution or upper bound
nodes.statement: If all the variables are integer in the solution, then we have the exact optimal solution. Otherwise, we obtain an infeasible solution, which produces an upper bound for the problem.
assumptions: If all the variables are integer in the solution
conclusions: then we have the exact optimal solution
Otherwise, we obtain an infeasible solution, which produces an upper bound for the problem

nodes.name: Sequential fixing yields a lower bound
nodes.statement: When the algorithm terminates, it produces a feasible solution that yields a lower bound for the objective value.
conclusions: it produces a feasible solution that yields a lower bound for the objective value

nodes.name: Sequential Fixing (SF) algorithm for OPT-CRV
nodes.statement: \caption{The Sequential Fixing Algorithm (SF) for Problem OPT-CRV} \begin{tabular}{ll} \hline 1 : & Relax integer variables $x_{i,j,m}^{l,h,r}$, $y_l^h$, and $n_l^h$; \\ 2 : & Solve the relaxed problem using a constrained NLP solver; \\ 3 : & {\bf if} (there is $y_l^h$ not fixed) \\ 4 : & $\;\;$ Find the largest $y_{l'}^{h'}$, where $[l',h']=\arg \max\{y_l^h\}$, \\ & $\;\;$ and fix it to $1$; \\ 5 : & $\;\;$ Fix other $y_l^h$'s according to constraint (\ref{eq:PathCon}); \\ 6 : & $\;\;$ Go to Step 2; \\ 7 : & {\bf end if} \\ 8 : & {\bf if} (there is $x_{i,j,m}^{l,h,r}$ not fixed) \\ 9 : & $\;\;$ Find the largest $x_{i',j',m'}^{l',h',r'}$, where $[i',j',m',l',h',r']=$ \\ & $\;\;$ $\arg \max\{x_{i,j,m}^{l,h,r}\}$, and set it to 1; \\ 10: & $\;\;$ Fix other $x_{i,j,m}^{l,h,r}$'s according to the constraints; \\ 11: & $\;\;$ {\bf if} (there is other variable that is not fixed) \\ 12: & $\;\;\;\;$ Go to Step 2; \\ 13: & $\;\;$ {\bf else} \\ 14: & $\;\;\;\;$ Fix $n_l^h$'s based on $\mathbf{x}$ and $\mathbf{y}$; \\ 15: & $\;\;\;\;$ Exit with feasible solution $\{\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{y},\mathbf{n}\}$; \\ 16: & $\;\;$ {\bf end if} \\ 17: & {\bf end if} \\ \hline \end{tabular}
nodes.statement_short: Repeatedly solve the relaxed NLP, fixing the largest path variable and then the largest channel variable to 1, until all are fixed.

nodes.name: Decomposition of OPT-CRV
nodes.statement: Since the domains of $x_{i,j,m}^{l,h,r}$ defined in (\ref{eq:OneChan1})$\sim$(\ref{eq:IntmFlow}) for different paths do not intersect with each other, we can decompose Problem OPT-CRV into two subproblems.
assumptions: the domains of $x_{i,j,m}^{l,h,r}$ defined in (\ref{eq:OneChan1})$\sim$(\ref{eq:IntmFlow}) for different paths do not intersect with each other

nodes.name: OPT-CS (channel scheduling)
nodes.statement: We have the {\em channel scheduling} problem (OPT-CS) as: \begin{eqnarray} && \hspace{-0.2in} H_l^h=\max_{\mathbf{x}} \sum_r \sum_m x_{z_l,z'_l,m}^{l,h,r}(1-p_{l,h}^r) \\ && \hspace{-0.2in} \mbox{subject to:} \; (\ref{eq:OneChan1})\sim(\ref{eq:IntmFlow}), \; x_{z_l,z'_l,m}^{l,h,r} \in \{0,1\}, \; \mbox{for all } l, h, r, m. \nonumber \end{eqnarray}
nodes.statement_short: On a chosen path, schedule channels into tunnels to maximize the expected number of successful tunnels.

nodes.name: OPT-PS (path selection)
nodes.statement: Letting $F_l^h = \log \left( 1 + \rho_l^T H_l^h \right)$, we have the following {\em path selection} problem (OPT-PS): \begin{eqnarray} \mbox{maximize:} && f(\mathbf{y}) = \sum_l \sum_h F_l^h y_l^h \\ \mbox{subject to:} && \sum_l\sum_{h \in \mathcal{P}_l} w_{l,h}^g y_l^h \le 1, \; \mbox{for all } \; g \nonumber \\ && y_l^h \in \{0,1\}, \; \mbox{for all } \; l, h. \nonumber \end{eqnarray}
nodes.statement_short: Select paths (binary $y_l^h$) to maximize $\sum F_l^h y_l^h$ subject to path constraints.

nodes.name: Optimal channel pairing for tunnels
nodes.statement: Consider three consecutive nodes along a path, denoted as nodes $i$, $j$, and $k$. Idle channels 1 and 2 are available at link $\{i, j\}$ and idle channels 3 and 4 are available at link $\{j, k\}$. Assume the packet loss rates of the four channels satisfy $p_{i,j}^1 > p_{i,j}^2$ and $p_{j,k}^3 > p_{j,k}^4$. To set up two tunnels, assigning channels \{1, 3\} to one tunnel and channels \{2, 4\} to the other tunnel achieves the maximum expectation of successful transmission on path section $\{i, j, k\}$.
assumptions: Consider three consecutive nodes along a path, denoted as nodes $i$, $j$, and $k$.
Idle channels 1 and 2 are available at link $\{i, j\}$ and idle channels 3 and 4 are available at link $\{j, k\}$.
Assume the packet loss rates of the four channels satisfy $p_{i,j}^1 > p_{i,j}^2$ and $p_{j,k}^3 > p_{j,k}^4$.
conclusions: assigning channels \{1, 3\} to one tunnel and channels \{2, 4\} to the other tunnel achieves the maximum expectation of successful transmission on path section $\{i, j, k\}$.
nodes.statement_short: Pairing best-with-best and worst-with-worst channels across consecutive links maximizes expected tunnel success.
nodes.label: th:th1

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 3 (channel pairing)
nodes.statement: Let the success probabilities on the channels be $\tilde{p}_{i,j}^1=1-p_{i,j}^1$, $\tilde{p}_{i,j}^2=1-p_{i,j}^2$, $\tilde{p}_{j,k}^3=1-p_{j,k}^3$, and $\tilde{p}_{j,k}^4=1-p_{j,k}^4$. We have $\tilde{p}_{i,j}^1 < \tilde{p}_{i,j}^2$ and $\tilde{p}_{j,k}^3<\tilde{p}_{j,k}^4$. Comparing the success probabilities of the channel assignment given in Theorem~\ref{th:th1} and that of the alternative assignment, we have $\tilde{p}_{i,j}^1 \tilde{p}_{j,k}^3 + \tilde{p}_{i,j}^2 \tilde{p}_{j,k}^4 - \tilde{p}_{i,j}^1 \tilde{p}_{j,k}^4 - \tilde{p}_{i,j}^2 \tilde{p}_{j,k}^3 =(\tilde{p}_{i,j}^1-\tilde{p}_{i,j}^2)(\tilde{p}_{j,k}^3-\tilde{p}_{j,k}^4) > 0$. The result follows.
nodes.statement_short: Compare success probabilities of the two pairings; the difference factors as a product of two same-sign differences.

nodes.name: Greedy tunnel construction is optimal
nodes.statement: According to Theorem~\ref{th:th1}, a greedy approach, which always chooses the channel with the lowest loss rate at each link when setting up tunnels along a path, produces the optimal overall success probability.
conclusions: a greedy approach, which always chooses the channel with the lowest loss rate at each link when setting up tunnels along a path, produces the optimal overall success probability

nodes.statement: Define the set of loss rates of the available channels on link $\{i, j\}$ as $\Lambda_{i,j}=\{p_{i,j}^m|m \in \Omega_{i,j} \}$.

nodes.name: OPT-rPS (relaxed path selection)
nodes.statement: To solve Problem OPT-PS, we first relax binary variables $y_l^h$ to allow them take real values in [0,1] and obtain the following {\em relaxed path selection} problem (OPT-rPS): \begin{eqnarray} \mbox{maximize:} && f(\mathbf{y}) = \sum_l \sum_h F_l^h y_l^h \\ \mbox{subject to:} && \sum_l\sum_{h\in \mathcal{P}_l} w_{l,h}^g y_l^h \le 1, \; \mbox{for all } \; g \nonumber \\ && 0 \leq y_l^h \leq 1, \; \mbox{for all } h,l. \nonumber \end{eqnarray}
nodes.statement_short: LP relaxation of OPT-PS with $0 \le y_l^h \le 1$.

nodes.name: Lagrangian of OPT-rPS
nodes.statement: We then introduce positive Lagrange Multipliers $e_g$ for the path selection constraints in Problem OPT-rPS and obtain the corresponding {\em Lagrangian function}: \begin{eqnarray} && \hspace{-0.45in} \mathcal{L}(\mathbf{y}, \mathbf{e}) = \sum_l\sum_h F_l^h y_l^h + \sum_g e_g (1 - \sum_l\sum_h w_{l,h}^g y_l^h) \\ && = \sum_l\sum_h ( F_l^hy_l^h - \sum_g w_{l,h}^g y_l^h e_g ) + \sum_g e_g \nonumber \\ && = \sum_l\sum_h \mathcal{L}_l^h ( y_l^h, \mathbf{e} )+ \sum_g e_g. \nonumber \end{eqnarray}

nodes.name: Lower-level per-path subproblem
nodes.statement: At the lower level, we have the following subproblems, one for each path $\mathcal{P}_l^h$, \begin{eqnarray} \max_{0 \leq y_l^h \leq 1} \mathcal{L}_l^h(y_l^h, \mathbf{e})=F_l^hy_l^h - \sum_g w_{l,h}^g y_l^h e_g. \end{eqnarray}
nodes.statement_short: For each path, maximize its Lagrangian term over $y_l^h \in [0,1]$ for fixed multipliers.

nodes.name: Relaxed dual problem
nodes.statement: At the higher level, by updating the dual variables $e_g$, we can solve the {\em relaxed dual problem}: \begin{eqnarray} \min_{\mathbf{e} \ge 0} \;\; q(\mathbf{e}) = \sum_l\sum_h \mathcal{L}_l^h \left( \left( y_l^h \right)^{\ast}, \mathbf{e} \right) + \sum_g e_g, \end{eqnarray} where $\left( y_l^h \right)^{\ast}$ is the optimal solution to (\ref{eq:FirstLevel}).
nodes.statement_short: Minimize the dual function $q(\mathbf{e})$ over nonnegative multipliers.

nodes.name: Subgradient method for Lagrange multipliers
nodes.statement: Since the solution to (\ref{eq:FirstLevel}) is unique, the relaxed dual problem (\ref{eq:SecondLevel}) can be solved using the following {\em subgradient method} that iteratively updates the Lagrange Multipliers~\cite{Bertsekas99}: \begin{eqnarray} e_g(\tau+1) = \left[ e_g(\tau)-\alpha(\tau)(1 - \sum_l\sum_h w_{l,h}^g y_l^h) \right]^+, \end{eqnarray} where $\tau$ is the iteration index, $\alpha(\tau)$ is a sufficiently small positive step size and $[x]^+$ denotes $\max\{x, 0\}$.
nodes.statement_short: Projected subgradient update of each multiplier $e_g$ with a small positive step size.

nodes.name: Distributed path selection algorithm
nodes.statement: \caption{Distribution Algorithm for Path Selection} \begin{tabular}{ll} \hline 1: & Initialization: set $\tau=0$, $e_g(0) >0 $ and step size $s \in [0,1]$; \\ 2: & Each source locally solves the lower level problem in (\ref{eq:FirstLevel}); \\ & {\bf if} ($F_l^h-\sum_g d_{l,h}^g e_g(\tau)) > 0$) \ $y_l^h=y_l^h+s$, $y_l^h= \min \{y_l^h,1\}$;\\ & {\bf else} \ \ $y_l^h=y_l^h-s$, $y_l^h=\max\{y_l^h,0\}$; \\ 3: & Broadcast solution $y_l^h(\mathbf{e}(\tau))$; \\ 4: & Each source updates $\mathbf{e}$ according to (\ref{eq:SubGrad}) and broadcasts $\mathbf{e}(\tau+1)$ \\ & through the common control channel; \\ 5: & $\tau \leftarrow \tau$+1 and go to Step 2 until termination criterion is satisfied; \\ \hline \end{tabular}
nodes.statement_short: Sources locally adjust path variables from current multipliers, broadcast them, and update multipliers by subgradient steps over the control channel until convergence.

nodes.name: Integrality of OPT-rPS optimum
nodes.statement: The optimal solution for the relaxed primal problem OPT-rPS in (\ref{eq:rPathSelec}) is also feasible and optimal for the original Problem OPT-PS in (\ref{eq:PathSelec}).
assumptions: The optimal solution for the relaxed primal problem OPT-rPS in (\ref{eq:rPathSelec})
conclusions: is also feasible and optimal for the original Problem OPT-PS in (\ref{eq:PathSelec}).
nodes.label: lemma:1

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 1
nodes.statement: According to Fact~\ref{thm:EqualCont}, the linearized problem of OPT-PS, i.e., OPT-rPS, can be rewritten as an equality constrained problem in the following form: \begin{eqnarray} \mbox{maximize:} && \mathbf{F}'\mathbf{y} \\ \mbox{subject to:} && \mathbf{w}_j' \mathbf{y}=1, \;\; j \in \mathcal{A}(\mathbf{y}^{\ast}) \\ && 0 \leq y_l^h \leq 1, \; \mbox{for all } h,l, \nonumber \end{eqnarray} where $\mathbf{F}$, $\mathbf{w}_j$'s, and $\mathbf{y}$ are column vectors with elements $F_l^h$, $w_{l,h}^g$, and $y_l^h$, respectively. We apply {\em Gauss-Jordan elimination} to the constraints in (\ref{eq:EqualCons1}) to solve for $\mathbf{y}$. Since there is not sufficient number of equations, some $y_l^h$'s are free variables (denoted as $y_i^f$) and the rest are dependent variables (denoted as $y_j^d$). Assuming there are $r$ free variables, the dependent variables can be written as linear combinations of the free variables after Gauss-Jordan elimination, as \begin{equation} y_j^d = \sum_{i=1}^r \bar{w}_j^i y_i^f + \bar{b}_j, \; j \in \mathcal{A}(y_i^{\ast}). \end{equation} Due to Gauss-Jordan elimination and binary vectors $\mathbf{w}_j$'s, $\bar{w}_j^i$ and $\bar{b}_j$ in (\ref{eq:depdent}) are all integers. Therefore, if all the free variables $y_i^f$ attain binary values, then all the dependent variables $y_j^d$ computed using (\ref{eq:depdent}) will also be integers. Since $0 \leq y_j^d \leq 1$, being integers means that they are either 0 or 1, i.e., binaries. That is, such a solution will be feasible. Next we substitute (\ref{eq:depdent}) into problem (\ref{eq:EqualCons}) to eliminate all the dependent variables. Then we obtain a unconstrained problem with only $r$ free variables, as \begin{equation} \mbox{maximize:} \;\; \sum_{i=1}^r \bar{F}_i y_i^f + \bar{b}_0 \end{equation} Since the free variables $y_i^f$'s take value in \{0, 1\}, this problem can be easily solved as follows. If the coefficient $\bar{F}_i > 0$, we set $y_i^f=1$; otherwise, if $\bar{F}_i < 0$, we set $y_i^f=0$. Thus (\ref{eq:GaussElimi}) achieves its maximum objective value. Once all the free variables are determined with their optimal binary values, we computes the dependent variables using (\ref{eq:depdent}), which are also binary as discussed above. Thus we obtain a feasible solution, which is optimal.
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to active equality constraints, apply Gauss-Jordan elimination with integer coefficients, and set free variables by coefficient sign to get a binary optimum.

nodes.name: Strong duality for OPT-rPS
nodes.statement: If the relaxed primal Problem OPT-rPS in (\ref{eq:rPathSelec}) has an optimal solution, then the relaxed dual problem (\ref{eq:SecondLevel}) also has an optimal solution and the corresponding optimal values of the two problems are identical.
assumptions: If the relaxed primal Problem OPT-rPS in (\ref{eq:rPathSelec}) has an optimal solution
conclusions: then the relaxed dual problem (\ref{eq:SecondLevel}) also has an optimal solution and the corresponding optimal values of the two problems are identical.
nodes.label: lemma:2

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 2
nodes.statement: By definition, the problems in (\ref{eq:LagFun}) and (\ref{eq:SecondLevel}) are primal/dual problems. The primal problem always has an optimal solution because it is bounded. Since Problem OPT-rPS is an LP problem, the relaxed dual problem is also bounded and feasible. Therefore the relaxed dual problem also has an optimal solution. We have the {\em strong duality} if the primal problem is convex, which is the case here since Problem OPT-rPS is an LP problem.
nodes.statement_short: Boundedness of the LP primal gives dual feasibility and attainment; LP convexity gives strong duality.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 4 from Lemmas 1 and 2
nodes.statement: We have Theorem~\ref{th:th2} on the optimality of the path selection solution, which follows naturally from Lemmas~\ref{lemma:1} and~\ref{lemma:2}.
nodes.statement_short: Combine integrality of the relaxed optimum (Lemma 1) with strong duality (Lemma 2).

nodes.statement:
(ii) {\em Optimality Bound}: This proof is extended from a result first shown in~\cite{Deb08} for layered videos. We first show a property of group utility $U_g(\vec{l})$, which will be used in the proof of the optimality gap. For two vectors $\vec{l}^1_g$ and $\vec{l}^2_g$, letting $\Delta = U_g(\vec{l}^1_g)-U_g(\vec{l}^2_g)$, we have  egin{eqnarray} & & \hspace{-0.2in} \Delta = \sum_{k=1}^M (n_{g,k}-n_{g,k+1}) 	imes \log \left( 1 +  rac{ \sum_{m=1}^k  eta_g b_{g,m}(l_{g,m}^1-l_{g,m}^2) }{ Q^b_g + \sum_{m=1}^k  eta_g b_{g,m} l_{g,m}^2 } ight) 
onumber \ & & \hspace{-0.2in} \le \sum_{k=1}^M \sum_{m=1}^k (l_{g,m}^1-l_{g,m}^2)^+(n_{g,k}-n_{g,k+1}) 	imes \log \left( 1+  eta_g b_{g,m} / \left[ Q^b_g+\sum_{m=1}^k  eta_g b_{g,m} l_{g,m}^2 ight] ight) 
onumber \ & & \hspace{-0.2in} \le \sum_{k=1}^M \sum_{m=1}^M (l_{g,m}^1-l_{g,m}^2)^+(n_{g,k}-n_{g,k+1}) 	imes \log \left( 1 +  eta_g b_{g,m} / \left[ Q^b_g + \sum_{m=1}^k  eta_g b_{g,m} l_{g,m}^2 ight] ight) 
onumber\ & & \hspace{-0.2in} = \sum_{m=1}^M (l_{g,m}^1-l_{g,m}^2)^+ \left[ U_g(\vec{l}^2_g+b_{g,m})-U(\vec{l}^2_g) ight], \end{eqnarray} where $y^+=\max \{ 0, y \}$. The first inequality is due to the concavity of logarithm functions. Next we prove the optimality bound. Let $\vec{l}_{t}$ be the output of GRD1 after $t$ iterations. Let the utility gap between the optimal solution and the GRD1 solution be $F_{t} = U(\vec{l}^{\ast}) - U(\vec{l}_{t})$, and $\vec{e}_{\hat{g},\hat{m}}(t)$ the argument found in Step 4 of GRD1 after $t$ iterations. onumber \ & & \hspace{-0.3in} \le \sum_g\sum_m (l_{g,m}^{\ast}-l_{g,m})^{+} [U(\vec{l}_{t-1}+\vec{e}_{g,m}(t))-U(\vec{l}_{t-1})] 
onumber \ & & \hspace{-0.3in} \le \sum_g\sum_m (l_{g,m}^{\ast}-l_{g,m})^{+} [U(\vec{l}_{t-1}+\vec{e}_{\hat{g},\hat{m}}(t))- U(\vec{l}_{t-1})]  rac{b_{g,m}+R/T_e}{b_{\hat{g},\hat{m}}(t)+R/T_e}
onumber \ & & \hspace{-0.3in} \le  rac{U(\vec{l}_t)-U(\vec{l}_{t-1})}{ b_{\hat{g}, \hat{m}}(t) + R/T_e} \sum_g\sum_m [l_{g,m}^{\ast}(b_{g,m}+R/T_e)]. 
onumber \end{eqnarray} The first inequality is due to (ef{eq:lema2}) and the second inequality follows Step 4 of GRD1. It follows (ef{eq:st1}) that $\sum_g\sum_m l_{g,m}^{\ast} \le T_e$ and $\sum_g\sum_m b_{g,m}l_{g,m}^{\ast} \le R$. We have $F_{t-1} \le (F_{t-1}-F_{t})  rac{2R}{b_{\hat{g}, \hat{m}}(t)+R/T_e}$. Solving for $F_t$, we have $F_{t}\le F_{t-1} \left\{ 1 - \left[ b_{\hat{g},\hat{m}}(t)+R/T_e ight] / (2R) ight\}$. Suppose the {\em WHILE} loop in Table~ef{tab:GreedyAlgo1} has been executed $k$ times when the solution is obtained.  egin{eqnarray} F_k &\le& F_{k-1} \left\{ 1-\left[b_{\hat{g},\hat{m}}(k)+R/T_eight] / (2R) ight\} 
onumber \ & \le & F_0 \prod_{t=1}^k \left\{ 1 - \left[ b_{\hat{g},\hat{m}}(t)+R/T_e ight] / (2R) ight\} 
onumber \ &\le& F_0 \left\{ 1 - 1/(2kR) \sum_{t=1}^k [ b_{\hat{g},\hat{m}}(t)+R/T_e ] ight\}^k. 
onumber \end{eqnarray} The {\em WHILE} loop exits when one or both of two constraints are violated. If $\sum_{g}\sum_{m} l_{g,m} \le T_e$ is violated, there is no tile that can be used. Therefore $k \ge T_e$ and $\sum_{t=1}^kR/T_e\ge R$. If constraint ``$A$ is not empty'' is violated, all the videos have been allocated sufficient number of tiles and will be transmitted at full rates. We have $\sum_{t=1}^k b_{\hat{g},\hat{m}}(t) \geq R$ in this case. It follows that  egin{eqnarray} F_k &\le& F_0 \left\{ 1 - 1/(2kR) \sum_{t=1}^k [ b_{\hat{g},\hat{m}}(t)+R/T_e ] ight\}^k 
onumber \ & \le & F_0 \left[ 1 - 1/(2k) ight]^k \; \le \; F_0 e^{-1/2}. 
onumber \end{eqnarray} Since $F_0=U(\vec{l}^{\ast})$, we have $U(\vec{l}_k)\ge(1-e^{-1/2})U(\vec{l}^{\ast})$. Therefore, we conclude that the GRD1 solution is bounded by $(1-e^{-1/2})U(\vec{l}^{\ast})$ and $U(\vec{l}^{\ast})$.

nodes.name: Swap gains reward
nodes.statement: We can further increase E[Reward] by switching the tile assignment, i.e., assign channel $i$ to $\xi_j$ and channel $j$ to $\xi_i$. With this new assignment, the net increase in E[Reward] is \begin{eqnarray} & & \hspace*{-0.3in} c_j(t)\mbox{Inc}(\xi_i) + c_i(t)\mbox{Inc}(\xi_j)-c_i(t)\mbox{Inc}(\xi_i)-c_j(t)\mbox{Inc}(\xi_j) \nonumber \\ & = & [c_j(t) - c_i(t)][\mbox{Inc}(\xi_i) - \mbox{Inc}(\xi_j)] > 0. \nonumber \end{eqnarray}
nodes.statement_short: Swapping the two assignments changes reward by a positive product
nodes.section: 4.2.3 Tile Scheduling in a Time Slot

nodes.name: Same ordering is optimal
nodes.statement: Therefore E[Reward] is maximized when the $\{ \mbox{Inc}(\xi_i) \}$ and $\{c_i(t)\}$ are in the same order.
nodes.statement_short: Hence optimal reward requires matching orderings

nodes.name: Success probabilities
nodes.statement: Let the success probabilities on the channels be $\tilde{p}_{i,j}^1=1-p_{i,j}^1$, $\tilde{p}_{i,j}^2=1-p_{i,j}^2$, $\tilde{p}_{j,k}^3=1-p_{j,k}^3$, and $\tilde{p}_{j,k}^4=1-p_{j,k}^4$. We have $\tilde{p}_{i,j}^1 < \tilde{p}_{i,j}^2$ and $\tilde{p}_{j,k}^3<\tilde{p}_{j,k}^4$.
nodes.statement_short: Introduce channel success probabilities and their order

nodes.name: Compare the two pairings
nodes.statement: Comparing the success probabilities of the channel assignment given in Theorem~\ref{th:th1} and that of the alternative assignment, we have $\tilde{p}_{i,j}^1 \tilde{p}_{j,k}^3 + \tilde{p}_{i,j}^2 \tilde{p}_{j,k}^4 - \tilde{p}_{i,j}^1 \tilde{p}_{j,k}^4 - \tilde{p}_{i,j}^2 \tilde{p}_{j,k}^3 =(\tilde{p}_{i,j}^1-\tilde{p}_{i,j}^2)(\tilde{p}_{j,k}^3-\tilde{p}_{j,k}^4) > 0$. The result follows.
nodes.statement_short: The difference of the two pairings factors into a positive product

nodes.name: Reduce to equality constraints
nodes.statement: According to Fact~\ref{thm:EqualCont}, the linearized problem of OPT-PS, i.e., OPT-rPS, can be rewritten as an equality constrained problem in the following form: \begin{eqnarray} \mbox{maximize:} && \mathbf{F}'\mathbf{y} \\ \mbox{subject to:} && \mathbf{w}_j' \mathbf{y}=1, \;\; j \in \mathcal{A}(\mathbf{y}^{\ast}) \\ && 0 \leq y_l^h \leq 1, \; \mbox{for all } h,l, \nonumber \end{eqnarray} where $\mathbf{F}$, $\mathbf{w}_j$'s, and $\mathbf{y}$ are column vectors with elements $F_l^h$, $w_{l,h}^g$, and $y_l^h$, respectively.
nodes.statement_short: By Fact 1 rewrite OPT-rPS with active constraints as equalities

nodes.name: Gauss-Jordan elimination
nodes.statement: We apply {\em Gauss-Jordan elimination} to the constraints in (\ref{eq:EqualCons1}) to solve for $\mathbf{y}$. Since there is not sufficient number of equations, some $y_l^h$'s are free variables (denoted as $y_i^f$) and the rest are dependent variables (denoted as $y_j^d$). Assuming there are $r$ free variables, the dependent variables can be written as linear combinations of the free variables after Gauss-Jordan elimination, as \begin{equation} y_j^d = \sum_{i=1}^r \bar{w}_j^i y_i^f + \bar{b}_j, \; j \in \mathcal{A}(y_i^{\ast}). \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Express dependent variables as linear combinations of free variables

nodes.name: Integrality of dependent variables
nodes.statement: Due to Gauss-Jordan elimination and binary vectors $\mathbf{w}_j$'s, $\bar{w}_j^i$ and $\bar{b}_j$ in (\ref{eq:depdent}) are all integers. Therefore, if all the free variables $y_i^f$ attain binary values, then all the dependent variables $y_j^d$ computed using (\ref{eq:depdent}) will also be integers. Since $0 \leq y_j^d \leq 1$, being integers means that they are either 0 or 1, i.e., binaries. That is, such a solution will be feasible.
nodes.statement_short: Integer coefficients make dependent variables binary when free ones are

nodes.name: Eliminate dependent variables
nodes.statement: Next we substitute (\ref{eq:depdent}) into problem (\ref{eq:EqualCons}) to eliminate all the dependent variables. Then we obtain a unconstrained problem with only $r$ free variables, as \begin{equation} \mbox{maximize:} \;\; \sum_{i=1}^r \bar{F}_i y_i^f + \bar{b}_0 \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Substitute to get an unconstrained linear problem in free variables

nodes.name: Optimize free variables by sign
nodes.statement: Since the free variables $y_i^f$'s take value in \{0, 1\}, this problem can be easily solved as follows. If the coefficient $\bar{F}_i > 0$, we set $y_i^f=1$; otherwise, if $\bar{F}_i < 0$, we set $y_i^f=0$. Thus (\ref{eq:GaussElimi}) achieves its maximum objective value.
nodes.statement_short: Set each free variable to 1 or 0 by the sign of its coefficient

nodes.name: Binary optimal solution
nodes.statement: Once all the free variables are determined with their optimal binary values, we computes the dependent variables using (\ref{eq:depdent}), which are also binary as discussed above. Thus we obtain a feasible solution, which is optimal.
nodes.statement_short: The resulting solution is binary, feasible and optimal

nodes.name: Primal/dual pair
nodes.statement: By definition, the problems in (\ref{eq:LagFun}) and (\ref{eq:SecondLevel}) are primal/dual problems.
nodes.statement_short: Identify the Lagrangian problem and the relaxed dual as a primal/dual pair

nodes.name: Existence of dual optimum
nodes.statement: The primal problem always has an optimal solution because it is bounded. Since Problem OPT-rPS is an LP problem, the relaxed dual problem is also bounded and feasible. Therefore the relaxed dual problem also has an optimal solution.
nodes.statement_short: Primal boundedness and LP structure give a dual optimum

nodes.name: Strong duality
nodes.statement: We have the {\em strong duality} if the primal problem is convex, which is the case here since Problem OPT-rPS is an LP problem.
nodes.statement_short: LP convexity gives equal optimal values

nodes.name: Subgradient equality
nodes.statement: Since $q(\mathbf{e}(\tau))$ is a linear function, we have subgradient equality, as \begin{eqnarray} q(\mathbf{e}(\tau))-q(\mathbf{e}^{\ast})= \left[ \mathbf{e}(\tau)-\mathbf{e}^{\ast} \right]'G(\tau). \nonumber \end{eqnarray}

nodes.name: Distance decreases

nodes.statement_short: The step-size condition makes the distance strictly decrease

nodes.name: Projection is nonexpansive
nodes.statement: Since the projection operation is {\em nonexpansive}, we have, \begin{eqnarray} && \hspace{-0.3in} ||\mathbf{e}(\tau+1)-\mathbf{e}^{\ast}|| = ||[\mathbf{e}(\tau)-\alpha(\tau)G(\tau)]^+-[\mathbf{e}^{\ast}]^+|| \nonumber \\ &\le& ||\mathbf{e}(\tau)-\alpha(\tau)G(\tau)-\mathbf{e}^{\ast}|| < ||\mathbf{e}(\tau)-\mathbf{e}^{\ast}||, \nonumber \end{eqnarray} which states the conditional convergence of the algorithm.
